frames.narration: Two generators start up. Each takes a lease on a free machine number from the registry: number 1 and number 2. They renew it regularly, and it expires if they die.
At millisecond 1,000 after the start date, the application on machine 1 saves an order. The generator reads its clock and builds the ID: time 1,000, machine 1, sequence 0.
The ID is 4,194,308,096. There was no network call and no waiting on any other machine. It is saved with the order.
In the same millisecond machine 2 also creates an ID. Same time, but its machine number is 2, so the ID is different: 4,194,312,192. Two machines never need to meet to avoid each other.
Machine 1 creates another ID in the same millisecond. The time and machine are the same, so the sequence part counts up: 1000 | 1 | 1. It could do this 4,096 times within a millisecond.

A millisecond later the time field has grown and the sequence starts again at 0. Every new ID is larger than the earlier ones, so rows are added at the end of the database index instead of at random places.
Now something goes wrong: a time-sync fix sets machine 1's clock back by 5 milliseconds. The generator compares the new time with the last one it used and sees it is earlier.
It refuses to issue IDs, since it could repeat ones it already gave out, and raises an alert. A few milliseconds later the clock passes the last value and it carries on. No duplicate was ever made.
